title: Feeding the Five Thousand
lead: What we have too little of will be enough once we give it to Jesus.
questions: What are your five loaves, the ones you still keep in the basket because “what difference will these make among so many?”
Which “it can’t be done” do you hide behind most often, and what would the matter look like if you started from what there is?
Who is the youngest or least significant person in your community whom no one has yet asked what they have in their basket?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: In yesterday’s reading the boat was sinking; in today’s the bread runs out. Apart from the resurrection, this is the only miracle of Jesus recorded by all four evangelists. The first church decided it could not be left out of any version of the story of Christ’s life. The story begins with exhaustion: the apostles return from their mission, and Jesus orders a rest in a solitary place. The plan collapses, because the crowd runs along the shore and gets there first. And then comes the sentence that makes this story worth reading carefully: Jesus “had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd.” These are words from Moses’ prayer for a successor to lead Israel. God answered it by giving Joshua, whose name in Greek is Jesus. The answer to Israel’s oldest prayer is standing on the shore, moved with compassion.

Toward evening the disciples suggest sending the people away, and Jesus answers: “You give them something to eat.” Philip does the math: two hundred denarii, eight months of a laborer’s wages, and still not enough. Andrew brings a boy, adding a comment we know from our own lives: five barley loaves and two fish, “but what difference will these make among so many?” Jesus doesn’t respond to the arithmetic. He has the people sit down in groups of hundreds and fifties, the way Israel was organized on the way out of Egypt, and for an hour He arranges a random crowd into the formation of a people fed with bread from heaven. It was also the largest shared meal with the unclean in all the Gospels: out in the wilderness no one could perform the ritual washing, and Jesus fed everyone until they were full without asking a single screening question. Twelve baskets of leftovers were gathered, “so that nothing will be wasted”: one for each of those who had said it couldn’t be done.

For this the crowd wanted to make Him king, so Jesus withdrew to a mountain. In the whole Gospel of John the word “king” appears sixteen times, and not once does Christ use it of Himself. The one title He never used is the very one they will accuse Him of before Pilate. The lesson for us is that sentence: “You give them something to eat.” He doesn’t demand what we don’t have. He asks only for the five loaves we do have, handed over into God’s hands.

In yesterday’s reading the boat was sinking. In today’s, just as the title of our section says, the bread runs out. The miracle we read about today is the only one recorded by all four evangelists, apart from the resurrection itself. The church of the first generations evidently believed that this one scene must not be left out of any version of the story of Jesus. It’s worth asking why it is so important.

sections.heading: A Vacation That Fell Through
paragraphs: The story begins by describing the disciples’ exhaustion. The apostles return from their first mission on their own, excited and worn out, and there is so much going on around Jesus that “they did not even have time to eat.” Christ makes a decision every overworked person should frame and hang on the wall: “Come with Me privately to a solitary place, and let us rest for a while.” God doesn’t glorify overwork. He Himself orders a retreat. Earlier on, Mark tells of the death of John the Baptist and of Herod’s interest in Jesus. That context may have added to the need to get away, but the evangelist gives the disciples’ rest as the main reason.

The plan for rest, however, collapses before the boat reaches the shore. People see where the disciples are heading and run along the lake to meet the Teacher. When Jesus steps ashore, the “solitary place” is already crowded. Then comes a sentence of great weight in this story: Jesus “had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd.” That is not a loose metaphor. The phrase clearly echoes the biblical picture of God’s people as a flock of sheep in need of a shepherd, found in the prophets and in the book of Numbers, where Moses asks God for a successor. The Creator answered Israel’s need then by giving it Joshua. And the name Joshua, in Hebrew Yehoshua, in Greek is Jesus. Mark is echoing the verse in which the plea for a shepherd found its fulfillment in a man bearing the same name as the One standing before the crowd. The answer to Israel’s oldest prayer appeared on the shore, moved with compassion.

It’s worth noticing, too, what Jesus did not do: He didn’t cancel the rest; He postponed it. Right after the feeding, Mark adds that Jesus made the disciples get into the boat, dismissed the crowd Himself and went up the mountain to pray. The crowd’s need was urgent, but the disciples’ exhaustion didn’t disappear just because a more pressing problem had come along. Anyone who serves others will find more pastoral wisdom in that detail than in many a handbook.

sections.heading: You Give Them Something to Eat
paragraphs: Toward evening the disciples come with a sensible proposal: send them away so they can buy food in the villages. Jesus’ answer sounds like a joke: “You give them something to eat.” There is a gentle irony in this command that is easy to miss. These men have just come back from a mission during which they healed the sick and drove out demons. Faced with disease, they acted with power; faced with a shortage of bread, they immediately switched to the language of accounting. Philip does the math in a flash: “Two hundred denarii would not buy enough bread,” and that was a laborer’s pay for eight months of work. The group’s treasury couldn’t cover even a token snack for a crowd like that. Then Andrew brings a boy, adding at once a caveat we often voice ourselves: “Here is a boy with five barley loaves and two small fish. But what difference will these make among so many?” Barley bread was the food of the poor, cheaper than wheat; two fish were a dried snack, not a food supply. The entire provision in this scene is a child’s basket of the cheapest food, presented with the comment “it’s not enough anyway.” Jesus doesn’t answer that comment with a single word. He tells the people to sit down.

sections.heading: In Hundreds and Fifties
paragraphs: Mark remembered the details of this seating: “the green grass,” groups “of hundreds and fifties.” The green grass is evidence that it was spring. John confirms that the Passover was near. The division into hundreds and fifties at once told those people something people today have to be reminded of. This is exactly how Israel was organized in the wilderness, on the way out of Egypt. It was not just the logistics of distribution, or at least not only that. For one hour a crowd of random people on the grass was arranged into the formation of a people coming out of slavery, fed with bread from heaven. Whoever sat in this scene was living through events from the book of Exodus.

Against the customs of the time one more thing becomes visible: this was the largest shared meal with the unclean that the Gospels record. Out in the wilderness no one had any way to observe the rules about ritual washing, and in a crowd of Galilean villagers many were regarded as permanently unclean. A devout teacher was not supposed to break bread with them. Jesus feeds them all at once and doesn’t ask anyone a single screening question. He satisfies their hunger, but He doesn’t screen the hungry in any way.

sections.heading: Twelve Baskets
paragraphs: Mark describes the miracle itself with verbs familiar from every Jewish table: He took, He blessed, He broke, He gave. The same four verbs will come back in the upper room over the bread of the Last Supper and at the table in Emmaus, when the disciples recognize the risen Lord. The feeding of the crowd carries an echo of God’s presence and blessing, revealed from Eden, through the manna in the wilderness, and in the Christian era through every Communion table, pointing ahead to the great feast in the Kingdom of God. On the grass by the lake there are no special effects: the multiplication happens somewhere between Jesus and the hands of the disciples handing out the food. And they “all ate and were satisfied,” five thousand men, and with women and children probably well over ten thousand people. God doesn’t hand out starvation rations; when He feeds, He gives until people are full. Then comes a command that sounds surprising from the lips of the One who has just created food out of nothing: “Gather the pieces that are left over, so that nothing will be wasted.” The One who has bread for free does not allow it to be wasted. Abundance and respect for crumbs don’t exclude each other: with God they go hand in hand. Twelve full baskets were collected. It’s hard not to notice that there were twelve disciples too. Each of those who an hour earlier had said “send them away” went back to the boat carrying his own basket of evidence.

sections.heading: The King Who Slipped Away
paragraphs: The crowd’s reaction is immediate and completely logical: a prophet who feeds people in the wilderness like Moses is a candidate for liberator. John writes that they were about to come and “make Him king by force.” In that century, a scene like this followed a well-worn script: wilderness prophets promising signs like those of Moses gathered huge crowds and ended up as crushed rebels. One of them, after Herod’s death, simply put a diadem on his own head. Jesus does the opposite: He withdraws to a mountain by Himself. In the whole Gospel of John the word “king” appears sixteen times, and not once does Jesus use it of Himself. Only before Pilate will He speak of His kingdom, and explain that it is not of this world. He refused a crown from the hands of the crowd because He had come for a different one: the one we will see woven of thorns a few days from now in our series. The hope He brought was not a political shortcut to a full stomach. It was a longer road, and it reached deeper than the hunger of a single afternoon.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: At the center of this story is a sentence aimed straight at us: “You give them something to eat.” The disciples had excellent arguments that it couldn’t be done: too little money, too little food, too late in the day. Jesus didn’t dispute their math. He asked for what there was. It was enough, and with a surplus that filled twelve baskets. He talks with us the same way when we say our community is too small, the budget too modest and the workers a handful. He doesn’t demand what we don’t have. He asks us to place the five loaves we do have into His hands. It is also worth noticing that Jesus fed a crowd full of ritually unclean people and set no conditions at all. A community that wants to be like Him feeds, welcomes and serves, and doesn’t set up checkpoints in front of the table. And then there is the boy. The only person in this scene who gave Jesus anything was a child with a basket of cheap food. No adult shared anything. Sometimes the youngest and poorest in a community are holding exactly what God wants to start a miracle with. The question is whether anyone will even take an interest in what they have.
